grades.name: Grade 1 · Foundations
grades.intro: The foundations: the endgames every player must know, the basic tactics, and the habits of calculation that everything else is built on.

lessons.title: The square of the pawn
lessons.rule: Draw the square from the pawn to its queening square. If your king can step inside it, it catches the pawn.

steps.text: A passed pawn runs on its own; the question is whether your king can catch it. Picture a square with the pawn on one corner and its queening square on another: here a5–a1–e1–e5. Your king on g2 is outside it, so even with White to move the pawn queens. The tablebases agree: this is lost.

Move the king one file closer, to f2, and it is a different game: one step puts it inside the square (e1, e2 or e3), and from there it reaches the pawn in time. No calculation needed, just the picture.

items.prompt: White to move. Catch the pawn.
White to move. Only two moves hold.
Black to move. Can your king catch the h-pawn?

steps.text: Now do it for real against perfect play: catch the pawn and hold the draw.

lessons.title: Forks
lessons.rule: Before every move, look for a square where one of your pieces attacks two targets at once, above all the king and something else.

steps.text: A fork is one piece attacking two things at the same time. The opponent can only save one. Knights are the classic forkers because their attacks are hard to see, but queens, pawns and even kings fork too. The best forks come with check, so there is no time to save the other piece.

lessons.title: Opposition
lessons.rule: Kings facing each other with one square between: the side that does NOT have to move holds the opposition, and it decides king-and-pawn endings.

lessons.title: Checks, captures, threats
lessons.rule: Before you move, list every check, every capture and every threat, for both sides. Choose only after the list is complete.

lessons.title: Pins and skewers
lessons.rule: A piece in front of a more valuable one can't move freely: attack it again. A valuable piece in front of a lesser one must move: hit it and take what is behind.

lessons.title: Key squares
lessons.rule: With a king two squares in front of its pawn (not a rook pawn), the pawn queens whoever is to move.

lessons.title: Quiet moves and defence
lessons.rule: When there is no forcing move, ask what your opponent wants, then find the quiet move that stops it or improves your worst piece.

lessons.title: Lucena: building a bridge
lessons.rule: Rook and pawn against rook, your king in front of the pawn: check to push the enemy king away, rook to the fourth rank, walk your king out and block the checks with your rook.

lessons.title: Blind steps
lessons.rule: Keep the position in your head: name where each piece goes, and check the squares it now attacks.

lessons.title: Remove the defender
lessons.rule: If one piece holds everything together, take it, chase it or lure it away, then strike what it was guarding.

lessons.title: Philidor: the third-rank defence
lessons.rule: Defending rook and pawn against rook: keep your rook on your third rank until the pawn steps onto it, then check from behind.

lessons.title: Mating patterns
lessons.rule: Know the shapes: back rank, smothered, two pieces against the king. Recognise them and the calculation is short.

lessons.title: Opening principles and traps
lessons.rule: In the opening: take the centre, develop knights and bishops towards it, castle, and connect the rooks. Before every move, check what your opponent's last move threatens.

lessons.title: Grade 1 checkpoint
lessons.rule: Passed Grade 1: the foundations are yours.

grades.name: Grade 2 · Technique
grades.intro: Technique is turning what you know into points: winning won endings, spotting the second tactic behind the first, and keeping control when the opponent fights back.

lessons.title: Queen against a pawn on the seventh
lessons.rule: Against a centre or knight pawn on the seventh, check and pin until the defender has to stand in front of his pawn, then bring your king one step closer. Rook and bishop pawns can be a draw because of stalemate.

lessons.title: Discovered attacks
lessons.rule: When one of your pieces stands in front of a queen, rook or bishop, moving it opens a second attack. Give the moving piece a job too: a check or a capture.

lessons.title: Outside and protected passed pawns
lessons.rule: An outside passed pawn wins by decoying the enemy king; a protected passed pawn wins by waiting. Push only when it gains something.

lessons.title: Candidate moves: look wider
lessons.rule: List your candidates before you calculate any of them, and put the move you'd least expect on the list.

lessons.title: In-between moves and x-rays
lessons.rule: Before you recapture, ask whether there is a stronger move first. A check or a threat in between can change the whole sequence.

lessons.title: Converting an extra piece
lessons.rule: When you're winning, take away counterplay first: secure your king, trade pieces (not pawns), and bring every piece into the game before you go for the kill.

lessons.title: Outflanking
lessons.rule: When the kings stand face to face and you can't take the opposition, go around: step to the side and approach from the flank.

lessons.title: Clearance and interference
lessons.rule: If one of your own pieces is in the way, move it with tempo. If an enemy line holds things together, put a piece across it.

lessons.title: Blind Steps: three moves deep
lessons.rule: In your head, update the whole board after every move, not just the piece that moved: check what it attacks now and what it no longer defends.

lessons.title: Rook against pawn
lessons.rule: Rook against pawn is a race: cut the enemy king off along a rank or file, then bring your own king. If the pawn is far advanced with its king beside it, count before you commit.

lessons.title: Attacking the castled king
lessons.rule: Count attackers against defenders around the king. When you have more, look for the sacrifice that removes the last defender.

lessons.title: Defending: the calm move
lessons.rule: Under attack, find the opponent's best threat first. Then look for the move that defends and improves at the same time, and trade attacking pieces when you can.

lessons.title: When nothing is forced
lessons.rule: In a quiet position, look for your worst piece and improve it, and ask what your opponent's next good move would be.

lessons.title: Grade 2 checkpoint
lessons.rule: Passed Grade 2: technique is yours.

grades.name: Grade 3 · Strategy
grades.intro: Strategy is knowing what to do when nothing is forced: which pawns to push, which pieces to trade, which endings to aim for and which to avoid.

lessons.title: Rook endings: defending from the side
lessons.rule: Against a rook's pawn with the enemy rook in front of it, attack the pawn from the side: your rook guards it from a distance and is ready to check the king when it comes out.

lessons.title: Passed pawns must be pushed
lessons.rule: A passed pawn grows stronger with every step: support it with pieces behind it, and use the threat of promotion to tie the opponent down.

lessons.title: Zugzwang
lessons.rule: Sometimes the best move is to pass. If every move of your opponent's makes things worse, spend a tempo and let him move.

lessons.title: Think First: the opponent's reply
lessons.rule: For every candidate, find your opponent's best answer before you decide. A move is only as good as the reply it allows.

lessons.title: Sacrifices that attract
lessons.rule: A sacrifice can drag a piece, often the king, onto a square where it gets hit. Look for squares where a capture would put the piece into a fork, a pin or a mating net.

lessons.title: Opposite-coloured bishops
lessons.rule: With bishops of opposite colours, the defender blockades on the squares his bishop controls; two pawns are often not enough. The attacker needs a second front: pawns far apart.

lessons.title: The exposed king
lessons.rule: An exposed king is a target for every piece. Open lines towards it, bring the queen, and look for checks that drag it further into the open.

lessons.title: Knight and bishop endings
lessons.rule: Bishops love open boards and pawns on both wings; knights love blocked pawns and outposts. In knight endings count tempi as in pawn endings; in bishop endings, put your pawns on the colour your bishop doesn't control.

lessons.title: Blind Steps: four moves deep
lessons.rule: Before a long line, fix the starting position in your mind as patterns (who attacks what), not as a list of squares.

lessons.title: Converting a small advantage
lessons.rule: A small advantage grows by improving your worst piece and creating a second weakness. Don't force things; give the opponent problems he can't solve.

lessons.title: Trapped pieces and quiet moves
lessons.rule: A piece with no safe squares is already lost: take its squares away first, then attack it. The quiet move that does this is often the hardest to see.

lessons.title: Mating patterns II
lessons.rule: Learn the mates by their shape: Arabian (rook and knight), Anastasia (knight and rook on the edge), hook, dovetail. Then look for longer forcing lines that end in them.

lessons.title: The isolated queen's pawn
lessons.rule: With the isolated d-pawn: attack, using the open lines and the e5/c5 (or e4/c4) outposts, and keep pieces on. Against it: blockade the square in front, trade pieces, and win the pawn in the ending.

lessons.title: Outposts
lessons.rule: An outpost is a square in the enemy half that no enemy pawn can attack. Put a knight there, protected by a pawn, and it dominates; take away your opponent's outposts before he gets there.

lessons.title: Good and bad bishops
lessons.rule: A bishop is bad when its own pawns are fixed on its colour. Put your pawns on the other colour, trade your bad bishop for the opponent's good piece, or open the position so it can breathe.

lessons.title: Grade 3 checkpoint
lessons.rule: Passed Grade 3: you play with a plan.

grades.name: Grade 4 · Mastery
grades.intro: Mastery means precision: technical endings you can win in your sleep, defence that holds hard positions, and calculation that stays accurate deep into a line.

lessons.title: Mate with two bishops
lessons.rule: Two bishops side by side build a wall the king can't cross. Shrink the box step by step with the king's help, drive the king to a corner, and watch out for stalemate.

lessons.title: Hard defence
lessons.rule: In a bad position, find the opponent's plan and make it as hard as possible to carry out: every obstacle is a chance for him to go wrong.

lessons.title: Rook endings: two against one
lessons.rule: Two pawns against one on the same side with rooks on the board is usually a draw. Keep your rook active and your king in front of the pawns.

lessons.title: Think First: deeper lines
lessons.rule: Calculate forcing lines to the end, until the position is quiet, then evaluate. Stopping in the middle of a sequence is how most miscalculations happen.

lessons.title: Quiet moves in sharp positions
lessons.rule: When forcing moves don't work, look for the quiet move that creates an unstoppable threat.

lessons.title: Queen against rook
lessons.rule: Queen beats rook: drive the king to the edge, aim for the position where the defender must move his rook away from his king, then fork or win it.

lessons.title: Pawn endings in depth
lessons.rule: In pawn endings, count. Count moves to queen, count tempi in the opposition battle, count spare pawn moves. Then play.

lessons.title: Deflection, x-ray and double check
lessons.rule: Overloaded defenders, pieces behind pieces, and double checks: when they appear together, the combination is usually deeper than it looks.

lessons.title: Blind Steps: five moves deep
lessons.rule: Long lines are held as a story, not as squares: who went where, and why.

lessons.title: Technique against resistance
lessons.rule: A won position against a fighting defender: keep checks under control, push your passed pawns with support, and don't allow a perpetual.

lessons.title: Promotion tricks and special moves
lessons.rule: Promotion isn't always to a queen, and en passant and castling can be tactics too. Check every special move in sharp positions.

lessons.title: Attacks on both wings
lessons.rule: When the kings castle on opposite sides, speed decides: open lines towards the enemy king with pawns, and count who arrives first.

lessons.title: Hanging pawns and the Carlsbad
lessons.rule: Hanging pawns are strong while they stand side by side; attack them so one has to advance, then blockade. In the Carlsbad structure, the side with the half-open c-file plays the minority attack (b4-b5).

lessons.title: Prophylaxis
lessons.rule: Before every move ask: what would my opponent play if it were his move? Then prevent it, if preventing it costs you nothing.

lessons.title: Grade 4 checkpoint
lessons.rule: Passed Grade 4: precision is yours.

grades.name: Grade 5 · Expert
grades.intro: The final grade: the hardest technical endings, defence in positions that look lost, and calculation at expert level.

lessons.title: Mate with bishop and knight
lessons.rule: Bishop and knight mate only in a corner of the bishop's colour. Drive the king to the edge, then walk it along the edge to the right corner with the knight and bishop together (the W manoeuvre).

lessons.title: Sacrifices at expert level
lessons.rule: Expert sacrifices pay for the initiative, not for a forced mate. Count what you get: tempo, open lines, a weak king, pieces out of play.

lessons.title: Rook and bishop against rook
lessons.rule: Rook and bishop against rook is usually a draw: keep your king off the edge, or near the corner the bishop doesn't control, and keep your rook active.

lessons.title: Think First: expert
lessons.rule: Use your candidate list as a checklist against your own blind spots: retreats, quiet moves, moves by pieces you haven't moved in a while.

lessons.title: Queen endings
lessons.rule: In queen endings, king safety and the passed pawn decide. Shelter your king from checks, and push your passed pawn when the queen can protect it from behind.

lessons.title: Defending the indefensible
lessons.rule: When the position is bad, look for the most stubborn defence and the practical trick. Many lost positions are drawn by the player who keeps setting problems.

lessons.title: The quiet killer
lessons.rule: At the top level the most dangerous move is often the quietest. Look for the move that takes away the opponent's last good option.

lessons.title: Blind Steps: master's lines
lessons.rule: The deepest visualization is built on the clearest picture of the starting position. Spend the first seconds on it.

lessons.title: Finishing the game
lessons.rule: The last part of a won game is the most dangerous. Play the safest winning move, not the prettiest.

lessons.title: Expert combinations
lessons.rule: Combine the ideas: attraction, clearance, deflection. The combination is the sum of patterns you already know.

lessons.title: Long mates
lessons.rule: Long mating combinations are a chain of checks: each one must take away squares or drive the king towards your pieces.

lessons.title: Endgame technique at expert level
lessons.rule: In endings, the right plan beats the right move: decide what you're aiming for (a won pawn ending, a passed pawn, a fortress), then find the moves.

lessons.title: One king, two jobs
lessons.rule: A king can head for two goals at once: a diagonal path towards one is just as short as a straight one, so walk diagonally and keep both threats alive.

lessons.title: Expert positional choices
lessons.rule: At the top level most games are decided by quiet decisions: which piece to improve, which pawn to fix, which trade to allow.

lessons.title: Final checkpoint
lessons.rule: Graduated from Plyra School.
